mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-01.stem: What does a digital display increment of 0.01 mm establish by itself?
options: The measurement error never exceeds 0.01 mm.
The instrument suits every product tolerance.
The smallest increment represented by the display.
reasons: Display resolution describes the display increment; it does not guarantee that actual measurement error stays within that increment.
Suitability for tolerance decisions also requires checking the instrument specifications, condition, measurement method and required tolerance.
0.01 mm is this instrument's smallest display increment, which is distinct from measurement accuracy.
A fine display does not justify skipping cleaning or checks of movement, gaps and play before use.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-02.stem: The closed caliper displays zero after resetting, but mechanical play remains. What is appropriate?
options: Check zero indication and mechanical play separately; report the abnormality.
Assume the play has disappeared because zero is displayed.
Keep rewriting measurements until the play disappears.
Use it for acceptance if the display increment is small.
reasons: Setting the displayed zero and removing physical play are different matters. Report remaining abnormalities and follow the approved checks.
Changing the display with a button does not prove that physical play has disappeared.
Rewriting measurement records does not remove play from the instrument.
The number of display digits alone guarantees neither instrument condition nor suitability for tolerance decisions.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-03.stem: What is mainly checked by holding the closed jaws up to the light?
reasons: Looking for light between the jaws is not a way to identify the workpiece material.
Check acceptance tolerances in drawings or specifications; do not determine them only from light between the jaws.
Looking for light between the jaws is not a battery-level test.
This check concerns gaps between closed jaws, which is different from checking the displayed zero.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-04.stem: When changing to another caliper, what should you do about its reading increment?
options: Assume it matches the previous instrument.
Check the specifications of the instrument now in use.
Choose the finest increment mentioned in the guide.
reasons: Similar-looking calipers do not necessarily have the same reading increment.
Check the specified scale arrangement and minimum reading of the instrument you have switched to.
The vernier examples in this material do not establish a 0.01 mm reading increment for every instrument.
Use the actual instrument specifications rather than arbitrarily choosing the smallest number in the material.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-05.stem: Besides the jaw gap, which preparation check does the guide describe?
options: Smooth slider movement and absence of play.
The selling price of the product.
The operator's ranking by measurement count.
Changing tolerances according to product colour.
reasons: Besides gaps, the material calls for checking smooth slider movement and the presence of play.
The selling price is not an item for checking slider condition before use.
Ranking the number of measurements does not replace checks for smooth movement and play.
This check does not permit changing an approved tolerance according to product colour.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-06.stem: A colleague says displaying zero proves the instrument has no abnormality. What needs correcting?
options: Zero indication removes the need to check tolerances.
Pressing the button removes dirt from measuring surfaces.
Zero indication alone does not prove the absence of gaps or play.
Zero indication makes instrument specifications unnecessary.
reasons: Even after setting the display to zero, check product tolerances and the decision method.
The zero button sets the display; it does not physically remove dirt from the measuring faces.
A zero display is only a display check; it does not prove that the jaws have no gap or play.
Setting the display to zero does not allow the instrument-specification check to be omitted.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-07.stem: Which vernier reading increments are listed in this guide?
reasons: 0.5 mm and 2 mm are not the combination of minimum vernier readings listed in this material.
The material lists vernier examples of 0.1 mm, 0.05 mm and 0.02 mm, not a specification shared by every model.
The combination of 1 mm, 0.01 mm and 0.001 mm does not match the vernier examples being asked about.
The combination of 0.01 mm, 0.005 mm and 0.002 mm does not match the vernier examples being asked about.

mfg1-caliper-supplement-check-08.stem: Does this paper-based supplement authorize adjustment of a real instrument?
options: Its explanation alone is enough to begin adjustment.
Every instrument uses the same adjustment method.
The zero button completes the adjustment.
The specified instrument's specifications and approved procedure must be checked.
reasons: Completing paper-based study does not authorise starting adjustments on a real instrument.
Do not apply one identical adjustment method to instruments with different construction and specifications.
Setting the displayed zero alone does not mean that all physical adjustments and pre-use checks are complete.
Before handling a real instrument, confirm that instrument's specifications, your authority and the approved procedure.

mfg38-mechanical-q001.stem: In Figure1, which panels correspond, in order, to no mobile phones, no electronic devices and no running?
reasons: In this schematic: H = no mobile-phone use; I = no electronic-device use; E = no running; this matches the required order.
At position 2, E means no running, whereas I (no electronic-device use) is required. At position 3, I means no electronic-device use, whereas E (no running) is required.
At position 1, I means no electronic-device use, whereas H (no mobile-phone use) is required. At position 2, H means no mobile-phone use, whereas I (no electronic-device use) is required.

At position 1, E means no running, whereas H (no mobile-phone use) is required. At position 2, H means no mobile-phone use, whereas I (no electronic-device use) is required. At position 3, I means no electronic-device use, whereas E (no running) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q002.stem: In Figure1, which panels correspond, in order, to no pedestrian access, do not touch and not for drinking?
reasons: At position 1, F means do not touch, whereas D (no admittance) is required. At position 2, D means no admittance, whereas F (do not touch) is required.
In this schematic: D = no admittance; F = do not touch; G = not drinkable; this matches the required order.
At position 2, G means not drinkable, whereas F (do not touch) is required. At position 3, F means do not touch, whereas G (not drinkable) is required.
At position 1, G means not drinkable, whereas D (no admittance) is required. At position 3, D means no admittance, whereas G (not drinkable) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q003.stem: In Figure1, which panels correspond, in order, to general prohibition, no smoking, no open flames and no entry (bar symbol)?
reasons: At position 2, C means no open flames, whereas B (no smoking) is required. At position 3, B means no smoking, whereas C (no open flames) is required.
At position 1, B means no smoking, whereas A (general prohibition) is required. At position 2, A means general prohibition, whereas B (no smoking) is required.
In this schematic: A = general prohibition; B = no smoking; C = no open flames; J = no entry; this matches the required order.
At position 1, J means no entry, whereas A (general prohibition) is required. At position 4, A means general prohibition, whereas J (no entry) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q004.stem: In Figure2, which panels correspond, in order, to fall hazard, slippery surface, electric shock, tsunami danger and rockfall/landslide?
reasons: At position 1, E means slip warning, whereas F (fall-from-height warning) is required. At position 2, F means fall-from-height warning, whereas E (slip warning) is required.
At position 3, I means tsunami danger, whereas H (electric-shock warning) is required. At position 4, H means electric-shock warning, whereas I (tsunami danger) is required.
At position 4, J means cliff-collapse/landslide warning, whereas I (tsunami danger) is required. At position 5, I means tsunami danger, whereas J (cliff-collapse/landslide warning) is required.
In this schematic: F = fall-from-height warning; E = slip warning; H = electric-shock warning; I = tsunami danger; J = cliff-collapse/landslide warning; this matches the required order.

mfg38-mechanical-q005.stem: In Figure2, which panels correspond, in order, to general warning, obstacle, step up, step down and overhead hazard?
reasons: In this schematic: A = general caution; B = obstacle warning; C = step-up warning; D = step-down warning; G = overhead warning; this matches the required order.
At position 1, B means obstacle warning, whereas A (general caution) is required. At position 2, A means general caution, whereas B (obstacle warning) is required.
At position 3, D means step-down warning, whereas C (step-up warning) is required. At position 4, C means step-up warning, whereas D (step-down warning) is required.
At position 2, G means overhead warning, whereas B (obstacle warning) is required. At position 5, B means obstacle warning, whereas G (overhead warning) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q006.stem: In Figure3, which panels correspond, in order, to flammability, corrosion, health hazard, aquatic environmental hazard and acute toxicity,skin or eye irritation and related hazards?
reasons: At position 2, C means health hazard, whereas B (corrosivity) is required. At position 3, B means corrosivity, whereas C (health hazard) is required.

In this schematic: A = flammability; B = corrosivity; C = health hazard; D = aquatic environmental hazard; E = exclamation mark for harmful acute toxicity, skin/eye irritation and related hazards; this matches the required order.
At position 1, D means aquatic environmental hazard, whereas A (flammability) is required. At position 4, A means flammability, whereas D (aquatic environmental hazard) is required.

At position 4, E means exclamation mark for harmful acute toxicity, skin/eye irritation and related hazards, whereas D (aquatic environmental hazard) is required. At position 5, D means aquatic environmental hazard, whereas E (exclamation mark for harmful acute toxicity, skin/eye irritation and related hazards) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q007.stem: In Figure4, which panels correspond, in order, to fire extinguisher, AED, wide-area evacuation site, evacuation building and tsunami evacuation location?
reasons: At position 1, B means automated external defibrillator (AED), whereas A (fire extinguisher) is required. At position 2, A means fire extinguisher, whereas B (automated external defibrillator (AED)) is required.

At position 3, D means evacuation site in a building, whereas C (wide-area evacuation site) is required. At position 4, C means wide-area evacuation site, whereas D (evacuation site in a building) is required.

mfg38-mechanical-q008.stem: You find Figure3 panel B on a container. What is appropriate?
options: Move your face close and identify it by smell.
Assume the sign authorizes all work.
Remove the hazardous sign and use it.
Check the hazard and prescribed handling in the label and SDS.
reasons: Bringing your face close to smell it may cause exposure. Identify it using the label, SDS and related information.
A hazard pictogram communicates danger; it does not authorise every task.
Removing the hazard sign does not remove the hazard and loses necessary information.
B is a corrosivity learning model. Check the label, SDS and specified handling conditions.

mfg38-mechanical-q009.stem: What is appropriate regarding Figure4 panel E?
options: Check the designated tsunami evacuation destination and route.
Assume every building is safe in a tsunami.
Treat it as unrestricted access permission.
Decide evacuation is unnecessary because you know the AED location.
reasons: This is a tsunami evacuation-site model, so confirm the designated destination and route.
The sign does not guarantee that every building is tsunami-safe.
An evacuation-site sign does not permit unrestricted entry into a caution area.
The AED location and the need for tsunami evacuation are separate decisions.

mfg38-mechanical-q010.stem: What is the reading in Figure5, in mm?
reasons: Omitting the sleeve's 0.5 mm gives 14.23 mm.
Adding the sleeve's 14.5 mm and thimble's 23× 0.01 mm gives 14.73 mm.
Do not concatenate 14.5 and 23 as digits; align the units and add them.
This value results from reading the sleeve as 15 mm; compare the reference line with the figure again.

mfg38-mechanical-q011.stem: What value is obtained by combining Figure6’s reference and deviation, in mm?
reasons: Treating the positive difference as negative and subtracting gives 19.88 mm.
This treats 12 divisions as 0.012 mm, contrary to the figure's 0.01 mm/division.
This uses only the reference value without adding the specified 12-division difference.

mfg38-mechanical-q012.stem: What value follows from Figure7’s signed scale and reference, in mm?
reasons: This adds a negative difference as if positive; follow the sign specified in the figure.
10.090 mm does not match the specified 5× 0.002 mm difference.
This subtracts 0.100 mm rather than the specified 5× 0.002＝0.010 mm.

mfg38-mechanical-q013.stem: In Figure8, a positive indication means a bore smaller than the reference. What is the bore diameter in mm?
reasons: Here the＋indication means a bore smaller than the reference, so 25.000−12× 0.001＝24.988 mm.
This directly adds the＋indication to the bore size, reversing the relationship specified in this figure.
This treats 12 divisions as 0.120 mm instead of using 0.001 mm/division.
This ignores the specified 12-division difference and gives only the reference value.

mfg38-mechanical-q014.stem: Which hole in Figure9 does not pass through to the opposite side?
reasons: B is a through hole opening on the opposite side, unlike bottomed hole A.
A has a bottom inside and does not open through the opposite side.
Combining A and B fails to distinguish a bottomed hole from a through hole.
It is not none of them: the figure shows a bottom in A.

mfg38-mechanical-q015.stem: Which hole in Figure9 passes through to the opposite side?
reasons: A has a bottom inside and does not pass through the opposite side.
Combining A and B wrongly includes the non-through hole A.
B opens on the opposite side and passes through.
It is not none of them: B passes through the opposite side.

mfg38-mechanical-q016.stem: What is the depth of hole A in Figure9, in mm?
reasons: The 6 in⌀6 is the hole diameter, not its depth.
16 is the plate thickness, not the depth to the bottom of hole A.
7 mm is the remaining bottom thickness: plate 16 mm minus hole depth 9 mm, not hole A's depth.
The dimension indicated as hole A's depth is 9 mm.

mfg38-mechanical-q017.stem: Under Figure10’s convention, which panel indicates the side opposite the arrow?
reasons: In this figure's convention, B's basic symbol is above the reference line and indicates the other side of the arrow.
Compare the symbol positions in A and B to distinguish arrow side and other side in this material's convention.
Do not treat arrow side and other side as both; choose the side corresponding to the symbol position.
Do not confuse C's broken-arrow designation with B's basic-symbol position relative to the reference line.

mfg38-mechanical-q018.stem: In Figure10 panel C, which member with a prepared groove is indicated by the bent arrow?
reasons: The broken arrow in C does not point to the left member's groove preparation.
The broken arrow points to the right member's groove preparation and designates that member.
Do not extend the designation to both members; identify the member at the arrow tip.
The broken arrow supplies a designation, so no designation is not appropriate.

mfg38-mechanical-q019.stem: What is the total length of the red segments in Figure11, in mm?
reasons: 90 mm is the span from the first red start to the final end:35× 2＋20, including two gaps; it is not the red-only total.
This adds the 35 mm start-to-start pitch three times, instead of adding three 20 mm red segments.
Three red segments of 20 mm give 20× 3＝60 mm.
45 mm is not three 20 mm red segments; count segment lengths separately from gaps.

mfg38-mechanical-q020.stem: What is the gap between adjacent red segments in Figure11, in mm?
reasons: 20 mm is the red-segment length, not the gap to the next segment.
35 mm is the start-to-start pitch and includes the red-segment length.
Subtract segment length from pitch to obtain the gap; do not add them.
The gap is 35 mm pitch minus 20 mm segment length, giving 15 mm.

mfg38-mechanical-q021.stem: What is the pitch between corresponding starts in Figure11, in mm?
reasons: The figure gives 35 mm between corresponding start positions.
15 mm is the gap between red segments, not the start-to-start pitch.
20 mm is the red segment's own length, not the start-to-start pitch.
60 mm is the total of three red segments, not the pitch between adjacent starts.

mfg1-electrical-mock-03-practical-q01.stem: In a paper example, the main scale reads 18 mm and the vernier fraction is 0.45 mm. A records 18.45 mm and B 18.90 mm. Which statement correctly identifies B's recording error and how acceptance should be judged?
options: B is correct because it convertsmm tocm.
B indicates a minimum reading of 0.05 mm, so it can be used directly as the measurement.
B adds the 0.45 mm fraction twice. Check the drawing's permissible range and acceptance method separately.
A and B are two ways of writing the same value, so both can be declared acceptable.
reasons: Recording 18.90 mm is not a mm-to-cm conversion; this confuses unit conversion with adding the fraction.
The 0.05 mm minimum reading is the scale increment, not B's 18.90 mm or this example's 0.45 mm fraction.
18＋0.45＝18.45 mm.18.90 mm adds the fraction twice. Separate dimension calculation from acceptance based on drawings and procedures.
18.45 mm and 18.90 mm are different values. Without the permissible range and decision method, acceptance cannot be confirmed.

mfg1-electrical-mock-08-practical-q02.stem: Consider a basic paper self-holding circuit using an ordinary non-latching relay. The start input has already returned. Power fails while the circuit is holding, then only the power supply returns. Which description fits this example?
options: Power loss releases self-holding, and restoring power alone does not restart it.
Because it is self-holding, the coil remains energised even without power.
Restoring power always causes automatic restart regardless of input conditions.
If a stop contact is present, state changes caused by power loss need not be considered.
reasons: In this basic example, power loss de-energises the coil and releases holding through its own contact. The start input has returned, so power restoration alone does not establish a start path.
Self-holding does not mean permanent coil energisation without power. This question assumes an ordinary non-latching relay.
The start input has already returned. Unconditional automatic restart on power restoration contradicts this example's conditions.
A stop contact alone does not justify ignoring states during power loss and restoration. Verify actual equipment's restart prevention and safety-function suitability separately.

mfg1-electrical-mock-09-practical-q03.stem: In an ideal point-charge model with the same medium and separation, both charges are initially positive. Their magnitudes stay unchanged, but one sign changes from positive to negative. How do force magnitude and direction change?
options: The force doubles and remains repulsive.
The force magnitude is unchanged and repulsion becomes attraction.
The force magnitude becomes 0 and no force acts.
The force magnitude is unchanged and remains repulsive.
reasons: Charge magnitudes, distance and medium are unchanged, so there is no condition for doubling the force. Unlike signs also change the direction to attraction.
The product of charge magnitudes, distance and medium are unchanged, so force magnitude stays the same. Like signs become unlike, changing repulsion to attraction.
Changing the sign does not set the charge magnitude to 0. Unlike charges attract.
The unchanged magnitude is correct, but unlike signs cause attraction rather than continued repulsion.
